gene_editing.abstract: Condensed Matter > Statistical Mechanics arXiv:2611.30527 (cond-mat) [Submitted on 23 Nov 2026] Title: Nonequilibrium Dynamics of R-loop Formation in the CRISPR-Cas9 System Authors: Yu Liu , Bing Miao View a PDF of the paper titled Nonequilibrium Dynamics of R-loop Formation in the CRISPR-Cas9 System, by Yu Liu and Bing Miao View PDF HTML (experimental) Abstract: The binding specificity of CRISPR-Cas9 is governed by the stepwise formation of an R-loop, in which the sgRNA displaces the nontarget DNA strand and hybridizes with the target strand in discrete base pair steps. Here we develop a nonequilibrium dynamics framework that models R-loop formation as a continuous-time Markov birth-death process over twenty base pairs. Each transition rate is derived from Eyring transition-state theory and the Bell model, and combines three physical contributions, i.e., the torsional strain generated by the B-form to A-form helical conversion at the unwinding front, a base stacking correction that couples neighboring base pairs, and the allosteric work supplied by Cas9 conformational changes. We further derive the entropy production of the process, which is decomposed into activation, stacking, torsional, and allosteric terms. The resulting prediction model uses no external thermodynamic database and reaches Spearman correlations of 0.84 and 0.82 in two independent libraries of dCas9-sgRNA mismatch variants measured in vivo. The mismatch-type dependence is carried by one twist deviation and one pairing weight per type. Our model recovers the seed region sensitivity, the PAM-proximal activity gradient, and the moderate cost of dDrG mismatches, while isolating the high-activity double mismatch tail as the regime in which the present free-energy mapping is inadequate. The framework gives quantitative predictions on how DNA supercoiling and sequence context modulate binding affinity, and provides a mechanistic basis for sgRNA design. Computer Science > Machine Learning arXiv:2611.29055 (cs) [Submitted on 21 Nov 2026] Title: Hypothesis Generation and Semantic Attribution in Inverse Perturbation Modeling Authors: Pascal Passigan , Manolis Kellis View a PDF of the paper titled Hypothesis Generation and Semantic Attribution in Inverse Perturbation Modeling, by Pascal Passigan and 1 other authors View PDF HTML (experimental) Abstract: Understanding gene regulatory relationships at scale can help identify intervention points and anticipate unintended effects, but connecting a black-box model's learned computation to biological knowledge remains difficult. We investigate whether a sparse, typed gene network can generate inspectable hypotheses for steering malignant transcriptional programs toward expression patterns associated with favorable prognosis. Using LINCS L1000 CRISPR/Cas9 profiles paired with matched plate controls, we train a graph neural network to recover the perturbed gene from baseline and endpoint expression. Nodes combine ProTrek-derived protein representations with expression features; edges encode signed regulatory relationships and other gene interactions. We use this inverse formulation to nominate interventions for a desired multigene expression change in a specified cancer-cell context, and use integrated gradients and conductance along a path from the cell baseline toward the requested endpoint to attribute each nomination to gene states, typed messages, and residual connections. In A549, the model nominates TTK although its expression is unchanged in the request; the account assigns supporting credit through the checkpoint-associated MAD1L1 relationship and opposing credit through the E2F4 transcriptional-regulatory channel. Across 333 screened nominations in nine held-out cell lines, request-path attribution shows positive line-averaged correspondence with finite message-deletion effects at every transition. Existing TTK knockout measurements show requested-direction agreement across other markers at the 98.2nd percentile (10 wells), and ten of seventeen measured cases in the illustrative screen meet the predefined support criterion. These analyses make competing biological accounts of a nomination examinable and open to experimental test. Computer Science > Machine Learning arXiv:2611.31227 (cs) [Submitted on 23 Nov 2026] Title: How Far Can Linear Go? BiPert, a Unified Framework for Single-Cell Perturbation Modelling Authors: Abhishek Sharma , Aleksej Zelezniak View a PDF of the paper titled How Far Can Linear Go? BiPert, a Unified Framework for Single-Cell Perturbation Modelling, by Abhishek Sharma and Aleksej Zelezniak View PDF HTML (experimental) Abstract: Understanding how genetic perturbations affect cellular behaviour is essential for studying gene function and regulatory mechanisms. Large-scale CRISPR screens measure these effects across thousands of genes, but cover relatively few cellular contexts. Predicting perturbation responses in unseen cell types and identifying perturbed genes from their transcriptional effects therefore remain challenging. Here, we show that both tasks can be addressed through a common linear decomposition of transcriptional responses into shared and perturbation-specific components. Building on this principle, we introduce BiPert, a simple linear framework for both forward perturbation prediction and inverse identification. For forward prediction, BiPert outperforms existing methods that use no external biological knowledge when predicting gene expression changes in unseen cell lines. Its few-shot extension, BiPert-FS, adapts to new cell lines using as few as ten measured perturbations. For inverse identification, BiPert-ID identifies perturbed genes from single-cell expression profiles, outperforming deep-learning methods in unseen cell lines and donors. We further show that perturbations whose effects transfer more consistently across cellular contexts are also easier to identify, even after controlling for perturbation effect size. Together, these results establish a connection between perturbation transfer and identification, and demonstrate that simple linear models provide strong, interpretable baselines for both tasks. Electrical Engineering and Systems Science > Signal Processing arXiv:2611.28741 (eess) [Submitted on 21 Nov 2026] Title: VEGA: A Scalable Software-Hardware Co-design for Genome Alignment using RVV Extension Authors: Weihong Xu , Shijie Xu , Qunyou Liu , Giovanni Ansaloni , Cheng Zhuo , David Atienza View a PDF of the paper titled VEGA: A Scalable Software-Hardware Co-design for Genome Alignment using RVV Extension, by Weihong Xu and 4 other authors View PDF HTML (experimental) Abstract: Dynamic programming (DP)-based genome sequence analysis is fundamental to computational genomics, but it remains computationally intensive as genomic data volumes continue to outpace Moore's Law. Existing hardware accelerators often sacrifice programmability and scalability across diverse alignment algorithms. In this work, we present VEGA, a scalable software-hardware co-design that accelerates genome alignment using RISC-V Vector extensions. VEGA introduces specialized vector instructions and three key innovations: a Forefront Stationary dataflow that minimizes off-chip memory access, intersequence parallelism that maximizes SIMD lane utilization, and custom ISA extensions that accelerate core alignment operations. Evaluations show that VEGA achieves up to 15.1x and 9.7x speedups for Edit Distance and Smith-Waterman algorithms over the Ara2-RVV vector baseline, sustaining 10.2x and 6.7x gains for 10kbp sequences. Post-synthesis results indicate only 1.0% area overhead compared to a standard RISC-V core, with performance-per-area efficiency rivaling specialized ASICs. VEGA thus achieves a balanced advancement in efficiency, programmability, and scalability for genome sequence alignment. Abstract RNA predates cells, but today it “lives” inside them. Most current RNA is short-lived, folded, and often edited from its chromosomal origins, but it governs its own phenotypes. Our guiding question for this article was: How did RNA adjust its life when the RNA world era came to an end? RNA has its practical execution side in the whole-cell systems setup, serving critical functions in metabolism, compartmentalization, and in the RNA–DNA–PROTEIN network, coupling information handling and different events of macromolecule production into a self-sustaining loop. Aligning with current views of cooperation, we find that RNA life is distributed across a population of information-bearing entities persisting by compatibility, with DNA serving as a long-term memory and proteins offering the catalytic reach. We suggest that the reproduction–survival (R/S) axis, relevant to higher organisms, is also manifested by RNA in many forms, including RNA primers, mRNAs, tRNAs, and rRNAs. Each of these has contrasting, highly adapted molecular phenotypes. Ultimately, we wish to emphasize the evolutionary narrative where “RNA did not lose” in exchange for DNA genes or otherwise. Ultimately, RNA just changed strategy, and in its various forms, it has an active and critically important presence in all cells at all times.
